Evidence: Gidget Foundation report, patient accounts, GP check-up data

Stated Claim / Post Context:
One in four mums report perinatal anxiety or depression

Perinatal anxiety and depression is affecting more mothers than previous estimates, with one in four reporting they experienced it during or after pregnancy.

Actual Article Body:
While waiting at a traffic light with her newborn in the back, Joy Adan started crying.

It had been an ordinary morning and she'd just dropped her other child at daycare.

But once her tears began flowing, they did not stop.

"I knew straight away this is not normal," she told AAP.

Ms Adan had recently visited a female GP for her six-week check-up after having her second child.

"I was in and out of that six-week check-up in not even 10 minutes," she said.

"She hadn't really clocked that anything was wrong but I felt like something was wrong, so I walked out of that feeling a bit disappointed."

She had deliberately gone to see a different GP, as their usual family doctor was a male and she hoped a woman would pick up on her symptoms better.

After speaking to her husband, she went back to the male GP, who said she likely had postnatal depression and anxiety and organised a mental health plan with a referral to a psychologist for 10 sessions.

Looking back, Ms Adan wished she'd been offered a mental health screening during her pregnancy.

"I think that's where there's a big gap, that's where some of the symptoms might start, and then they compound once the baby is in your arms," she said.

"There's also a gap at that six-week check up, I didn't feel adequately understood or supported."

More than one in four (28 per cent) pregnant and postpartum mothers experience perinatal anxiety or depression, according to a report from Women's Mental Health Australia and Gidget Foundation Australia.

The figures, released on Tuesday, represent an increase in prevalence from one in five mothers, as previously estimated by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

Twenty per cent felt their mental health was inadequately supported at their six-week postpartum check-up, and 27 per cent said they continued to experience severe psychological distress nine to 12 months after giving birth.

Perinatal mental health not-for-profit Gidget Foundation has witnessed year-on-year increases in demand for their services, which includes free psychological support, chief executive Arabella Gibson said.

Ahead of Perinatal Mental Health Week November 22 to 28, she is calling for a national framework that strengthens screening, referral pathways and follow-up through pregnancy and 12 months after birth.

"Those 12 months after birth are really significant, it's not just 'the baby blues'," Ms Gibson said.
